                                     PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE                      §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LOAD INTERCONNECTION                               §                  OF TEXAS
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                       §


               TEXAS PUBLIC POWER ASSOCIATION’S RESPONSE TO
                        PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION


       The Texas Public Power Association (TPPA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the
proposal for publication (PFP) issued by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)
relating to the implementation of large load interconnection standards under Public Utility
Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.0561. These comments are submitted on behalf of TPPA and do not
necessarily reflect the opinions of any individual TPPA member.

       Formed in 1978, TPPA is the statewide association for the 72 municipally owned utilities
(MOUs) in Texas. TPPA membership also includes several electric cooperatives and joint action
agencies, as well as the Lower Colorado River Authority. TPPA members serve urban, suburban,
and rural Texas and vary in size from large, vertically-integrated utilities to relatively small
distribution-only systems. We are proud to serve approximately 5.1 million Texans across the state.
Most of our members operate within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region,
though several are located within either the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) or Midcontinent
Independent System Operator (MISO) region. MOUs offer a long track record of stability, and we
serve an essential role in providing secure and reliable power to the wholesale electricity markets
in these regions, including ERCOT. Many of our member systems have been providing stable and
reliable electric service to communities in Texas for over 100 years, and collectively, our members
provide more than 13,000 MW of generation and maintain more than 8,500 miles of high-voltage
transmission assets or more than 15% of the transmission in ERCOT.

       On March 12, 2026, the Commission issued a PFP, seeking comments by April 17, 2026.
These responses are timely filed.




TPPA Comments                                                                         Page 1 of 13
                                    I.      General Comments

       TPPA appreciates the work the Commission and its Staff have put into this project,
including the multiple discussion drafts, workshops, and stakeholder discussions undertaken by
the Commission, its Staff, and ERCOT.

Costs and Fees

       As noted in TPPA’s comments filed on April 13, 2026, in Project No. 58484, TPPA
believes legislative discussions surrounding SB6 made clear that residential and small commercial
customers should not bear costs associated with interconnecting large loads. Significant
transmission upgrades are being planned within ERCOT to support large load interconnections,
and although these upgrades may provide some system-wide benefits, they are primarily driven by
large load requests and are not necessary to directly serve residential and small commercial
customers; accordingly, those customers should not be responsible for such costs. TPPA believes
discussions regarding cost causation and recovery should occur in Project No. 58484; however,
certain elements in this rulemaking, including the $50,000/MW non-refundable interconnection
fee and the assignment of that fee and retained financial security to a TSP’s rate base, appear to
address the same cost causation and cost recovery issues under consideration in that project.. With
respect to financial security for system upgrades, TPPA remains concerned about the complexity
of assigning costs for facilities that serve the broader system to a single customer. While TPPA
supports requiring large load customers to pay the costs they create, the appropriate mechanism
for doing so should be determined in Project No. 58484 through transmission cost allocation and
rate design discussions.

       Ultimately, if the Commission chooses to address issues around cost causation and
recovery in this project, rather than Project No. 58484, then TPPA generally supports the fees and
financial security proposed throughout the rule and opposes any further reductions to these fees
and security. The proposal establishes multiple points at which a large load must provide funds,
either as fees or financial security. During the intermediate agreement phase, a large load customer
would be required to provide a study fee, financial security at a rate of $50,000/MW, and financial
security for any long-lead-time facilities that an interconnecting TSP procures on the customer’s
behalf. The study fee is intended to cover the costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP,
interconnecting TSP, and ERCOT in evaluating the interconnection request, consistent with PURA

TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 2 of 13
 § 37.0561(f). The $50,000/MW financial security requirement aligns with PURA § 37.0561(h),
which requires large loads to provide satisfactory proof of financial commitment. In addition,
PURA § 37.0561(h) requires financial security to cover advance payments for significant
equipment or services.

       During the interconnection agreement phase, large loads would be required to pay a
$50,000/MW non-refundable interconnection fee and to update the financial security posted during
the intermediate phase to cover significant equipment or services, contribution in aid of
construction (CIAC), and financial security for system upgrade costs. As proposed, the non-
refundable fee would offset the interconnecting TSP’s rate base. The CIAC would cover all direct
interconnection costs incurred by the TSP, while financial security for system upgrade costs would
help ensure that upgrades that are undertaken ultimately become used and useful.

       Notably, all financial security provided under the proposed rule would be refundable. As a
result, the only non-refundable costs borne by a large load customer would be the study fee, the
interconnection fee, and the CIAC for direct interconnection costs. TPPA believes it is appropriate
for large loads to bear these costs and supports requiring a substantial level of financial security in
addition to these fees. The proposed financial security requirements will help ensure that entities
seeking interconnection in ERCOT demonstrate a genuine and actionable intent to proceed. Given
ongoing challenges in distinguishing viable projects from speculative requests, these requirements
represent a reasonable and necessary safeguard.

       Though TPPA supports the proposed amounts, it recognizes large load concerns regarding
the level of financial security required during the intermediate phase. TPPA proposes an alternative
approach under which only 75% of the total requested peak demand would be subject to the
$50,000/MW financial security requirement during the intermediate phase. The remaining 25%
would be assessed at the same rate during the interconnection phase. This approach would reduce
the upfront financial burden on large loads while still ensuring sufficient security to deter
speculative projects from disrupting the ERCOT system.

       Additionally, TPPA notes that, as currently proposed, there appears to be overlap among
the fees requiring large loads to provide a CIAC, financial security for the procurement of
significant equipment and services, and financial security for system upgrades. For example, a
large load may provide financial security during the intermediate phase to cover a TSP’s

TPPA Comments                                                                            Page 3 of 13
 procurement of a breaker and then be required during the interconnection phase to provide
additional funds under the CIAC for that same breaker. Similarly, other long-lead-time equipment
procured by the TSP for system upgrades could fall under both the requirement for financial
security for significant equipment and services and the requirement for financial security for
system upgrades.

Offsets to Interconnecting TSP’s Rate Base

         Throughout the proposed rule, several mechanisms would result in the interconnecting TSP
offsetting its rate base with funds provided by large loads. 1 Under these subsections, amounts
collected from large loads would be paid to the interconnecting TSP and applied as an offset to the
TSP’s rate base in the earlier of its next interim or comprehensive rate proceeding.

         TPPA notes the potential overlap between these provisions and ongoing discussions in
Project No. 58484 regarding transmission cost of service. While TPPA does not oppose including
these paragraphs, we do not view them as a substitute for the broader issues being considered in
that project. TPPA therefore requests that the preamble to the PFA clearly state that adoption of
these provisions, which have received limited substantive discussion to date, does not materially
resolve or address the issues under consideration in Project No. 58484. TPPA believes these
concepts would be more appropriately and thoroughly addressed within that proceeding, where the
focus is on transmission cost recovery, rather than within this rulemaking, which has primarily
centered on interconnection processes.

         Additionally, if the proposed provisions for financial security and the non-refundable
interconnection fee are adopted, TPPA recommends that funds collected through these
mechanisms be issued to DSPs as a bill credit for further allocation to benefit end-use customers,
rather than being used to reduce a TSP’s rate base. As proposed, applying these funds to reduce a
TSP’s rate base may result in under-recovery of their costs, particularly when accounting for the


1
  Proposed § 25.194(f)(9) creates a non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000/MW covers study costs and
ensures the large load has financial commitment to prevent withdrawal. Funds collected under this fee will be paid
to the interconnecting TSP to offset their rate base. Proposed § 25.194(g)(4) provides that if a large load withdraws,
financial security first covers costs already incurred by the interconnecting DSP and interconnecting TSP, 20% of the
remaining balance is refunded to the large load, and the remaining 80% is applied to the interconnecting TSP’s rate
base. Proposed § 25.194(h)(4) provides that for underutilized capacity, any remaining financial security, after the
interconnecting DSP and interconnecting TSP costs are covered, is refunded 20% to the large load, with the
remaining 80% applied to the interconnecting TSP’s rate base.


TPPA Comments                                                                                         Page 4 of 13
 cost of capital required to finance their transmission projects. Allocating the funds to DSPs to be
used for the benefit of end-use customers would preserve proper TSP cost recovery while
providing tangible benefits to end-use customers. Ideally, bill credits would be distributed to DSPs
in a manner that benefits all end-use customers in ERCOT; and TPPA is eager to work with other
stakeholders to find the most fair way to accomplish this goal.

                            II.     Recommendations by Subsection

       Proposed § 25.194(a) provides that “nothing in this section limits the authority of a
municipally owned utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for
large load customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.”
TPPA appreciates and supports the inclusion of this provision, as it is consistent with PURA
§ 37.0561(1).

       Proposed § 25.194(c)(3) defines “contracted peak demand” as the total demand requested
by a large load customer. TPPA recommends clarifying that contracted peak demand may not
always reflect the amount initially requested, but instead the amount ultimately approved by the
interconnecting DSP, interconnecting TSP, and the large load customer at the time the
interconnection agreement is executed.

       Proposed § 25.194(d) requires that a large load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and
the interconnecting TSP execute an intermediate agreement prior to the start of the interconnection
study phase. The rule further provides that the intermediate agreement must specifically identify
each entity’s responsibilities under this section, including which entity will accept the study fee
and financial security from the large load customer.

       TPPA agrees that the intermediate agreement should clearly specify whether the large load
customer is to report to the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP for purposes of paragraphs
(d)(1)–(11). This clarification will reduce confusion for both the large load customer and the
interconnecting entities by ensuring that each party understands which requirements it is
responsible for tracking and verifying.

       TPPA also recommends requiring the intermediate agreement to specify (1) which entity
the large load customer must notify in the event of a withdrawal of all or a portion of its requested
or contracted peak demand, and (2) which entity, whether the DSP or TSP, is responsible for


TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 5 of 13
 notifying the large load customer of a failure to utilize capacity in accordance with its phased
energization schedule.2

         Proposed § 25.194(d)(1) establishes site control requirements that large load customers
must meet to enter into an intermediate agreement. Specifically, proposed § 25.194(d)(1)(A)
requires a large load customer to demonstrate a signed or executed lease agreement with a duration
of at least five years from the date the customer is expected to reach contracted peak demand for
the parcel on which the proposed facility will be located. Proposed § 25.194(d)(1)(C) provides an
alternative method of demonstrating site control through a signed and executed agreement that
includes an option to purchase or lease the land.

         TPPA supports the inclusion of paragraph (C). However, for both paragraphs (A) and (C),
TPPA recommends requiring that such agreements extend for at least 15 years from the date the
large load customer is expected to reach contracted peak demand, with options to renegotiate terms
at the five-year mark. This recommendation is intended to align with the objectives of SB 6 and
the Commission’s goal of ensuring that infrastructure developed to serve large loads does not
become stranded in the event a customer exits the market before the end of the useful life of the
facilities constructed to serve it.3

         Proposed § 25.194(d)(2)(D) provides that ERCOT may request, and the large load
customer must provide, any information the customer claims is competitively sensitive. This
provision appears within the subsection addressing the intermediate agreement and the reporting
of substantially similar interconnection requests.4

         TPPA supports the inclusion of this requirement but believes it has broader applicability
than its current placement suggests. Rather than limiting its scope to information related to


2
  Proposed § 25.194(f) similarly requires the large load customer, interconnecting DSP, and interconnecting TSP to
execute an interconnection agreement prior to initiating the large load’s interconnection. TPPA recommends that
similar requirements be included under subsection (f) to specify (1) which entity the large load customer must notify
in the event of a withdrawal request, and (2) which entity, whether the DSP or TSP, is responsible for notifying the
large load customer of a failure to meet its phased energization schedule.
3
 TPPA recommends applying similar language to proposed § 25.194(f)(1), which address site control requirements
for large loads at the interconnection agreement phase.
4
  Notably, proposed § 25.194(f)(2)(D) addresses the reporting of substantially similar interconnection requests
during the interconnection agreement phase and includes a provision allowing ERCOT to request confidential
information. TPPA notes that if its recommendation to create a new subsection is adopted, paragraph (f)(2)(D) would
no longer be necessary.

TPPA Comments                                                                                         Page 6 of 13
 substantially similar interconnection requests at the intermediate agreement stage, TPPA
recommends relocating this provision to a separate subsection. This revision would clarify that
ERCOT may request competitively sensitive information at any point during the interconnection
process and with respect to any relevant information, not solely information concerning
substantially similar interconnection requests.

        Proposed § 25.194(d)(6) requires large load customers to report information regarding
backup generating facilities, defined as “generation facilities or energy storage facilities that are
not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in parallel with the ERCOT system and
cannot export energy to the ERCOT system.”5 TPPA supports this requirement but recommends
broadening it to also include reporting of plans for backup generation capable of exporting to the
grid, as well as plans for co-located generation. Including this information would be materially
useful in completing interconnection studies, providing the interconnecting DSP and
interconnecting TSP with a comprehensive view of the large load customer’s plans for backup and
co-located self-supply generation.

        Proposed § 25.194(d)(7) requires large load customers to disclose how they plan to
procure power. TPPA notes that Texas law provides that end-use customers cannot directly
procure power except under limited circumstances; instead, power is provided through either a
REP in competitive areas or the NOIE (MOU or electric cooperative) serving the customer’s
territory. Accordingly, TPPA recommends deleting paragraph (d)(7). As noted above, TPPA
further recommends requiring large load customers to provide additional information regarding
plans for export-capable backup generation and co-located generation.

        Given concerns about water use by data centers, TPPA also recommends that this provision
require disclosure about how the large load will procure water, including whether the large load’s
water needs will differ substantially year-to-year.

        Proposed § 25.194(d)(8) requires large load customers to disclose whether “it can be”
modeled as a controllable load resource. TPPA recommends clarifying this provision to require
the large load to explicitly indicate whether it intends to pursue registration with ERCOT as a


5
  Proposed § 25.194(f)(6) similarly requires disclosure at the time of executing the interconnection agreement. TPPA
recommends that this disclosure also include information on export-capable backup generation and co-located self-
supply generation.

TPPA Comments                                                                                        Page 7 of 13
 controllable load resource. Under current ERCOT stakeholder discussions, controllable load
resources may receive prioritization in interconnection timelines. As currently phrased, a large
load stating that it “can be” modeled as a controllable load resource does not commit to registering
as such but could still potentially benefit from any prioritization afforded to controllable load
resources. Clarifying the paragraph would ensure transparency and prevent ambiguity regarding
the large load’s intent and potential advantages in the interconnection process.

       Proposed § 25.194(d)(9) requires a large load to pay a standardized study fee of $100,000
if its requested peak demand is greater than or equal to 75 MW and less than 250 MW, and
$300,000 if its requested peak demand exceeds 250 MW. The paragraph further provides that these
values will be updated every five years based on changes in the consumer price index. Finally, it
provides that if the actual cost of completing the study exceeds the standardized fee, the large load
is responsible for paying the additional costs.

       TPPA supports requiring large loads to cover any costs incurred by the interconnecting
DSP, interconnecting TSP, or ERCOT that exceed the standardized fee collected to complete the
studies. TPPA also supports updating the standardized study fee based on the consumer price index
but recommends allowing for additional adjustments where study costs have historically increased
at a rate greater than the consumer price index.

       Proposed § 25.194(d)(10)(C)(ii) provides that a large load customer may satisfy its
financial security requirements using cash, a corporate or parental guaranty, or a letter of credit.
Historically, ERCOT and the Commission have emphasized uniform financial security
requirements to maintain financial integrity and avoid preferential treatment among market
participants. TPPA supports rules implemented neutrally and consistently across all participants.

       TPPA notes that ERCOT market participants may currently use cash or letters of credit to
satisfy financial security requirements, but, as of September 15, 2022, corporate and parental
guarantees are no longer accepted for market participation. If the Commission intends to permit
extension of unsecured credit in the form of corporate and parental guarantees for large load
customers entering interconnection agreements, TPPA recommends that the Commission also
permit the prudent extension of unsecured credit to all ERCOT market participants in all ERCOT
credit support situations, where the market participant or its guarantor meets appropriate credit



TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 8 of 13
 rating requirements. An example of such a situation is the requirement of credit support for QSE
operations’ invoicing and settlement.

        Proposed § 25.194(d)(10)(D) provides that if a large load customer uses a corporate or
parental guaranty, the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP may request financial records
or statements to assess the customer’s financial standing. TPPA supports the inclusion of this
provision as it provides additional safeguards against misuse of corporate and parental guarantees.
TPPA recommends clarifying that if the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP is not
satisfied with the financial stability of the corporate or parental guaranty, it is not required to accept
that form of financial security. TPPA recommends the following redline: “If the large load
customer provides a corporate or parental guaranty under this subsection, the interconnecting DSP
or interconnecting TSP may require the submission of financial records or statements to determine
the customer’s financial stability. If the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP determines
that the guaranty does not provide sufficient assurance, it is not required to accept that form of
financial security.”6

        Proposed § 25.194(f) requires a large load customer, interconnecting DSP, and
interconnecting TSP to enter into an interconnection agreement not later than 30 days after
completion of the interconnection study for the large load customer. Notably, several provisions
required under subsection (d) regarding the intermediate agreement are not included in subsection
(f).

        First, TPPA recommends that certain information requirements be carried forward into the
interconnection agreement, including information on power supply as required under subsection
(d)(7), as well as water supply, and whether the load will be a controllable load resource as required
to be reported under subsection (d)(8), as these are important details that remain relevant at the
interconnection stage.7




6
 TPPA further recommends that this proposed redline also apply to proposed (e)(8)(D) and (e)(10)(B) regarding the
use of corporate or parental guaranties in the interconnection agreement.
7
  Notably, TPPA recommends revisions to subsection (d)(7) regarding power supply, including information on water
supply, and to subsection (d)(8) regarding the reporting of controllable load status. TPPA further recommends that
these revised requirements be carried forward and included in subsection (f).


TPPA Comments                                                                                       Page 9 of 13
        Additionally, TPPA recommends that the interconnecting DSP, interconnecting TSP, and
the large load customer have at least 120 days to enter into the interconnection agreement after
completion of the interconnection study.

       Proposed § 25.194(f)(7) requires a large load customer to pay a non-refundable
interconnection fee of $50,000/MW of contracted peak demand. TPPA supports the inclusion of
this fee, as it appropriately balances the market’s need to ensure sufficient financial commitment
from the customer and to discourage withdrawal later in the process, which could disrupt the
broader market.

       Proposed § 25.194(f)(7)(B) provides that the non-refundable interconnection fee must be
paid to the interconnecting TSP and applied as an offset to the TSP’s rate base in the earlier of its
next interim or comprehensive rate proceeding. TPPA previously addressed this paragraph under
its general recommendations, recommending that the offset should be applied as a bill credit from
TSPs to DSPs, rather than by reducing the rate base of TSP. TPPA also stressed that this non-
refundable interconnection fee should not be treated as a resolution to the issues currently under
discussion in Project No. 58484.

       Proposed § 25.194(f)(9) requires a large load customer to pay all direct interconnection
costs through CIAC, “with no standard or other allowance offered to offset the customer’s CIAC
payments.” TPPA supports the Commission’s clarification that any interconnection allowances
previously offered by some TSPs are no longer necessary, ensuring a consistent interconnection
process across ERCOT. However, TPPA believes the current wording is unclear, as it does not
explicitly specify that it is addressing the interconnection allowances previously provided by
certain TSPs. To that end, TPPA recommends the following redline: “a large load customer must
pay all direct interconnection costs through CIAC, with no standard or other allowance offered to
offset the customer’s CIAC payments and no TSP may offer any allowance or other mechanism
to reduce a large load customer’s interconnection costs.”

       Proposed § 25.194(f)(9)(A) provides that CIAC will cover direct interconnection costs,
including all costs associated with facilities built to connect the large load customer to the existing
ERCOT system. TPPA supports requiring large load customers to pay for all direct costs and
believes the Commission has appropriately and clearly identified which costs qualify as direct
interconnection costs.

TPPA Comments                                                                           Page 10 of 13
        Proposed § 25.194(h)(1) requires the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP to
notify ERCOT if a large load fails to meet any part of its phased energization schedule by more
than six months. TPPA recommends clarifying that this requirement applies only to the initial
interconnection agreement established by the large load and does not toll for any amended
interconnection agreement that may revise the energization schedule. This clarification would
ensure that large loads cannot repeatedly amend their interconnection agreement to extend their
energization schedule in order to avoid forfeiting their financial security.

       TPPA further requests the Commission define “phased energization” as it is unclear
whether this references the interconnection process, building timelines, or a large load’s
energization ramp schedule.

       Proposed § 25.194(h)(4) provides that if a large load does not utilize their entire requested
capacity in accordance with their energization schedule, then the interconnecting TSP should apply
80% of the large load customer’s financial security to offset their rate base. TPPA previously
addressed this paragraph under its general recommendations, recommending that the offset should
be applied as a bill credit from TSPs to DSPs, rather than by reducing the rate base of TSPs.

       Proposed § 25.194(h)(6) provides that ERCOT must reallocate non-utilized capacity. If
the Commission adopts this proposed provision, any reallocation should be conducted through a
formal ERCOT-administered process; however, it is TPPA’s preference that such process should
not permit the reassignment of load or capacity to entities without the agreement of the affected
TSP.

       Proposed § 25.194(i) provides the terms for the refund of financial security for a large load
customer that energizes. Specifically, paragraph (1) states, “after applying financial security to any
outstanding amounts owed, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must refund 20%
of the remaining balance when the large load customer energizes and ratably as the large load
customer meeting the milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased energization of
its contracted peak demand.”

       TPPA requests that this paragraph be clarified to specify that the “remaining balance”
refers to all financial security collected by the interconnecting DSP and TSP from the large load
customer, excluding amounts applied to outstanding costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP or
TSP. TPPA further requests clarification that, after all outstanding balances of the interconnecting

TPPA Comments                                                                          Page 11 of 13
 DSP and TSP have been satisfied and 20% of the remaining balance has been refunded upon
energization, then the rest of the financial security, “the remaining 80% balance,” of the financial
security will be refunded ratably in accordance with the customer’s phased energization milestones.



                                        III.    Conclusion

       At this time, TPPA has no additional comments on the proposal for publication.

       TPPA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. As always, TPPA looks
forward to working with the Commission, Commission Staff, and stakeholders on this important
discussion in the coming months.




Dated: April 17, 2026
                                               Respectfully,

                                               ____________________
                                               Mariah Benson
                                               Regulatory Affairs Manager
                                               Texas Public Power Association
                                               PO Box 82768
                                               Austin, Texas 78708
                                               (512) 472-5965

TPPA Comments                                                                        Page 12 of 13
                 Texas Public Power Association’s (TPPA) Executive Summary

•   Broader issues related to cost allocation and recovery should be addressed in Project No. 58484 rather
    than in this rulemaking. Cost causation principles should ensure that large load customers pay for the
    infrastructure they require, even if those upgrades provide incidental system-wide benefits.
•   The proposed rule appropriately includes multiple financial commitments, including a study fee,
    financial securities, an interconnection fee, and CIAC; TPPA does not recommendation a reduction in
    the level of these fees, unless significant changes are made to the transmission cost of service
    allocation methodology in Project No. 58484. Further, TPPA requests clear language in the PFA’s
    preamble stating that these provisions do not resolve the broader cost allocation issues being
    considered in Project No. 58484.
•   TPPA notes that a number of the financial commitments may result in duplicative charges across
    CIAC, financial security for equipment and services, and financial security for system upgrades.
•   TPPA opposes applying collected funds to offset a TSP’s rate base because it may lead to under-
    recovery of costs and distort financial incentives. Instead, TPPA recommends distributing these funds
    to DSPs as bill credits to benefit end-use customers more directly and equitably. Ideally, these bill
    credits should be structured to benefit customers across ERCOT.
•   The definition of contracted peak demand should be clarified to reflect the final approved demand
    rather than the initially requested amount.
•   Intermediate agreements should clearly identify which entity (DSP or TSP) is responsible for
    receiving payments, enforcing requirements, communicating with the large load customer, and for the
    large load customer to report any withdrawals of capacity.
•   TPPA supports site control requirements but recommends extending minimum agreement terms to 15
    years, with an option to renegotiate after five years.
•   ERCOT’s authority to request competitively sensitive information should apply broadly across the
    interconnection process rather than being limited to specific provisions.
•   Reporting requirements should be expanded to include export-capable backup generation and co-
    located generation to improve system planning and study accuracy.
•   TPPA recommends requiring disclosure of water sourcing and variability.
•   TPPA recommends removing the requirement for large loads to disclose how they will procure
    power, as this is not consistent with how power is supplied in MOU service territories.
•   Large loads should be required to explicitly state whether they intend to register as controllable load
    resources rather than simply indicating that they could do so.
•   Key disclosures required during the intermediate phase, such as water supply and controllable load
    status, should also be required in the final interconnection agreement.
•   Study fees should be adjusted over time to reflect inflation and actual cost increases.
•   If parental guarantees are allowed for large loads, similar flexibility should be extended to other
    market participants that meet appropriate credit standards.
•   DSPs and TSPs should have the authority to reject parental guarantees if they are not satisfied with
    the guarantor’s financial standing.
•   TPPA supports the $50,000/MW non-refundable interconnection fee as an appropriate mechanism to
    ensure commitment and discourage late-stage project withdrawal.
•   TPPA supports requiring large loads to pay all direct interconnection costs through CIAC with no
    allowances or offsets provided by TSPs.
•   TPPA recommends clarifying that phased energization requirements apply only to the original
    interconnection agreement and cannot be avoided through repeated amendments. The term “phased
    energization” should be clearly defined.
•   TPPA recommends that ERCOT be required to develop the reallocation of unused capacity processes
    through the stakeholder process.

                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT LARGE                      §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LOAD INTERCONNECTION                               §                  OF TEXAS
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                       §


               TEXAS PUBLIC POWER ASSOCIATION' S RESPONSE TO
                        PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION


       The Texas Public Power Association (TPPA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the
proposal for publication (PFP) issued by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)
relating to the implementation of large load interconnection standards under Public Utility
Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.0561. These comments are submitted on behalf of TPPA and do not
necessarily reflect the opinions of any individual TPPA member.

       Formed in 1978, TPPA is the statewide association for the 72 municipally owned utilities

(MOUs) in Texas. TPPA membership also includes several electric cooperatives and joint action
agencies, as well as the Lower Colorado River Authority. TPPA members serve urban, suburban,
and rural Texas and vary in size from large, vertically-integrated utilities to relatively small
distribution-only systems. We are proud to serve approximately 5.1 million Texans across the state.
Most of our members operate within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region,
though several are located within either the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) or Midcontinent
Independent System Operator (MISO) region. MOUs offer a long track record of stability, and we
serve an essential role in providing secure and reliable power to the wholesale electricity markets

                                    I.      General Comments

       TPPA appreciates the work the Commission and its Staff have put into this proj ect,

Costs and Fees

       As noted in TPPA's comments filed on April 13, 2026, in Project No. 58484, TPPA
believes legislative discussions surrounding SB6 made clear that residential and small commercial
customers should not bear costs associated with interconnecting large loads. Significant
transmission upgrades are being planned within ERCOT to support large load interconnections,
and although these upgrades may provide some system-wide benefits, they are primarily driven by
large load requests and are not necessary to directly serve residential and small commercial
customers; accordingly, those customers should not be responsible for such costs. TPPA believes
discussions regarding cost causation and recovery should occur in Project No. 58484; however,
certain elements in this rulemaking, including the $50,000/MW non-refundable interconnection
fee and the assignment of that fee and retained financial security to a TSP' s rate base, appear to
address the same cost causation and cost recovery issues under consideration in that project.. With
respect to financial security for system upgrades, TPPA remains concerned about the complexity
of assigning costs for facilities that serve the broader system to a single customer. While TPPA
supports requiring large load customers to pay the costs they create, the appropriate mechanism
for doing so should be determined in Project No. 58484 through transmission cost allocation and
rate design discussions.

       Ultimately, if the Commission chooses to address issues around cost causation and
recovery in this proj ect, rather than Project No. 58484, then TPPA generally supports the fees and
financial security proposed throughout the rule and opposes any further reductions to these fees
and security. The proposal establishes multiple points at which a large load must provide funds,
either as fees or financial security. During the intermediate agreement phase, a large load customer
would be required to provide a study fee, financial security at a rate of $50,000/MW, and financial
security for any long-lead-time facilities that an interconnecting TSP procures on the customer' s
behalf. The study fee is intended to cover the costs incurred by the interconnecting DSP,
interconnecting TSP, and ERCOT in evaluating the interconnection request, consistent with PURA

 § 37.0561(f). The $50,000/MW financial security requirement aligns with PURA § 37.0561(h),
which requires large loads to provide satisfactory proof of financial commitment. In addition,
PURA § 37.0561(h) requires financial security to cover advance payments for significant
equipment or services.

       During the interconnection agreement phase, large loads would be required to pay a
$50,000/MW non-refundable interconnection fee and to update the financial security posted during
the intermediate phase to cover significant equipment or services, contribution in aid of
construction (CIAC), and financial security for system upgrade costs. As proposed, the non-
refundable fee would offset the interconnecting TSP's rate base. The CIAC would cover all direct
interconnection costs incurred by the TSP, while financial security for system upgrade costs would
help ensure that upgrades that are undertaken ultimately become used and useful.

       Notably, all financial security provided under the proposed rule would be refundable. As a
result, the only non-refundable costs borne by a large load customer would be the study fee, the
interconnection fee, and the CIAC for direct interconnection costs. TPPA believes it is appropriate
for large loads to bear these costs and supports requiring a substantial level of financial security in
addition to these fees. The proposed financial security requirements will help ensure that entities
seeking interconnection in ERCOT demonstrate a genuine and actionable intent to proceed. Given
ongoing challenges in distinguishing viable projects from speculative requests, these requirements
represent a reasonable and necessary safeguard.

       Though TPPA supports the proposed amounts, it recognizes large load concerns regarding
the level of financial security required during the intermediate phase. TPPA proposes an alternative
approach under which only 75% of the total requested peak demand would be subj ect to the
$50,000/MW financial security requirement during the intermediate phase. The remaining 25%
would be assessed at the same rate during the interconnection phase. This approach would reduce
the upfront financial burden on large loads while still ensuring sufficient security to deter
speculative projects from disrupting the ERCOT system.

       Additionally, TPPA notes that, as currently proposed, there appears to be overlap among
the fees requiring large loads to provide a CIAC, financial security for the procurement of
significant equipment and services, and financial security for system upgrades. For example, a
large load may provide financial security during the intermediate phase to cover a TSP' s

Offsets to Interconnecting TSP's Rate Base

         Throughout the proposed rule, several mechanisms would result in the interconnecting TSP
offsetting its rate base with funds provided by large loads. 1 Under these subsections, amounts
collected from large loads would be paid to the interconnecting TSP and applied as an offset to the
TSP' s rate base in the earlier of its next interim or comprehensive rate proceeding.

         TPPA notes the potential overlap between these provisions and ongoing discussions in
Project No. 58484 regarding transmission cost of service. While TPPA does not oppose including
these paragraphs, we do not view them as a substitute for the broader issues being considered in
that proj ect. TPPA therefore requests that the preamble to the PFA clearly state that adoption of
these provisions, which have received limited substantive discussion to date, does not materially
resolve or address the issues under consideration in Proj ect No. 58484. TPPA believes these
concepts would be more appropriately and thoroughly addressed within that proceeding, where the
focus is on transmission cost recovery, rather than within this rulemaking, which has primarily
centered on interconnection processes.

         Additionally, if the proposed provisions for financial security and the non-refundable
interconnection fee are adopted, TPPA recommends that funds collected through these
mechanisms be issued to DSPs as a bill credit for further allocation to benefit end-use customers,
rather than being used to reduce a TSP's rate base. As proposed, applying these funds to reduce a
TSP' s rate base may result in under-recovery of their costs, particularly when accounting for the

       Proposed § 25.194(a) provides that "nothing in this section limits the authority of a
municipally owned utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for
large load customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section."
TPPA appreciates and supports the inclusion of this provision, as it is consistent with PURA
§ 37.0561(1).

       Proposed § 25.194(c)(3) defines "contracted peak demand" as the total demand requested
by a large load customer. TPPA recommends clarifying that contracted peak demand may not
always reflect the amount initially requested, but instead the amount ultimately approved by the
interconnecting DSP, interconnecting TSP, and the large load customer at the time the
interconnection agreement is executed.

       Proposed § 25.194(d) requires that a large load customer, the interconnecting DSP, and
the interconnecting TSP execute an intermediate agreement prior to the start of the interconnection
study phase. The rule further provides that the intermediate agreement must specifically identify
each entity' s responsibilities under this section, including which entity will accept the study fee
and financial security from the large load customer.

       TPPA agrees that the intermediate agreement should clearly specify whether the large load
customer is to report to the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP for purposes of paragraphs
(d)(1)-(11). This clarification will reduce confusion for both the large load customer and the
interconnecting entities by ensuring that each party understands which requirements it is
responsible for tracking and verifying.

       TPPA also recommends requiring the intermediate agreement to specify (1) which entity
the large load customer must noti fy in the event of a withdrawal of all or a portion of its requested
or contracted peak demand, and (2) which entity, whether the DSP or TSP, is responsible for

                  Texas Public Power Association's (TPPA) Executive Summary

•   Broader issues related to cost allocation and recovery should be addressed in Project No. 58484 rather
    than in this rulemaking. Cost causation principles should ensure that large load customers pay for the
    infrastructure they require, even ifthose upgrades provide incidental system-wide benefits.
•   The proposed rule appropriately includes multiple financial commitments, including a study fee,
    financial securities, an interconnection fee, and CMC; TPPA does not recommendation a reduction in
    the level of these fees, unless significant changes are made to the transmission cost of service
    allocation methodology in Project No. 58484. Further, TPPA requests clear language in the PFA's
    preamble stating that these provisions do not resolve the broader cost allocation issues being
    considered in Project No. 58484.
•   TPPA notes that a number of the financial commitments may result in duplicative charges across
    CMC, financial security for equipment and services, and financial security for system upgrades.
•   TPPA opposes applying collected funds to offset a TSP's rate base because it may lead to under-
    recovery of costs and distort financial incentives. Instead, TPPA recommends distributing these funds
    to DSPs as bill credits to benefit end-use customers more directly and equitably. Ideally, these bill
    credits should be structured to benefit customers across ERCOT.
•   The definition of contracted peak demand should be clarified to reflect the final approved demand
    rather than the initially requested amount.
•   Intermediate agreements should clearly identify which entity (DSP or TSP) is responsible for
    receiving payments, enforcing requirements, communicating with the large load customer, and for the
    large load customer to report any withdrawals of capacity.
•   TPPA supports site control requirements but recommends extending minimum agreement terms to 15
    years, with all option to renegotiate after five years.
•   ERCOT's authority to request competitively sensitive information should apply broadly across the
    interconnection process rather than being limited to specific provisions.
•   Reporting requirements should be expanded to include export-capable backup generation and co-
    located generation to improve system planning and study accuracy.
•   TPPA recommends requiring disclosure of water sourcing and variability.
•   TPPA recommends removing the requirement for large loads to disclose how they will procure
    power, as this is not consistent with how power is supplied in MOU service territories.
•   Large loads should be required to explicitly state whether they intend to register as controllable load
    resources rather than simply indicating that they could do so.
•   Key disclosures required during the intermediate phase, such as water supply and controllable load
    status, should also be required in the final interconnection agreement.
•   Study fees should be adjusted over time to reflect inflation and actual cost increases.
•   If parental guarantees are allowed for large loads, similar flexibility should be extended to other
    market participants that meet appropriate credit standards.
•   DSPs and TSPs should have the authority to reject parental guarantees ifthey are not satisfied with
    the guarantor's financial standing.
•   TPPA supports the $50,000/MW non-refundable interconnection fee as an appropriate mechanism to
    ensure commitment and discourage late-stage project withdrawal.
•   TPPA supports requiring large loads to pay all direct interconnection costs through CMC with no
    allowances or offsets provided by TSPs.
•   TPPA recommends clarifying that phased energization requirements apply only to the original
    interconnection agreement and cannot be avoided through repeated amendments. The term "phased
    energization" should be clearly defined.
•   TPPA recommends that ERCOT be required to develop the reallocation ofunused capacity processes
    through the stakeholder process.
